sections.heading: Furnace and AC Trouble in Lincoln, and What Usually Causes It
body: Most no-heat and no-cooling calls trace back to one failed part, not a dead system. Here is what we look at first.

items.title: The furnace clicks but never lights
items.text: Usually a worn igniter or a dirty flame sensor. Both are small parts, and both are a short repair once the cause is confirmed.

items.title: It runs a few minutes, then shuts off
items.text: A clogged filter can make a furnace overheat and shut itself down. A flame sensor that can't prove the burner lit does the same thing.

items.title: The air conditioner hums but won't start
items.text: A weak capacitor is a common cause. It is one of the smallest repairs in the trade.

items.title: The air from the vents isn't cold
items.text: Low refrigerant means a leak, and a frozen coil points to airflow. Topping off refrigerant without finding the leak only buys time.

items.title: A new bang, squeal or rattle
items.text: Don't ignore a new noise. A technician can tell you whether it's a loose part or something bigger, and a blower motor usually complains before it quits.

tail: When it is one of these, the answer is a part. The whole system is a separate question, and it comes second.

sections.quote: Another company in town told us we would be spending a minimum of $2,000 to just fix it and they really thought a whole new system would be more appropriate. After having Comfort Techs come look at problem, the issue was resolved for a small fraction of the cost the other company had quoted us.

sections.heading: What Usually Goes Wrong With a Central Air Conditioner
body: Most no-cooling calls come down to a short list of parts. Ice on the refrigerant line, water around the indoor unit, an outdoor fan that isn't spinning or a breaker that trips every time the system starts are all worth a call.
If you see ice or water, turn the system off and call. Running a struggling air conditioner can turn a small repair into a bigger one.

items.title: A weak capacitor
items.text: The capacitor gives the compressor and the fan motor the jolt they need to start. When it weakens, the unit hums and won't run. It is among the most common and least expensive repairs.

items.title: A dirty coil or a clogged filter
items.text: Dust and a choked filter cut airflow until the coil freezes into a block of ice. Thawing it is the easy part. Finding out why it got that way is the repair.

items.title: Low refrigerant
items.text: An air conditioner doesn't use refrigerant up. Low means a leak, and adding more without fixing the leak only buys a few weeks.

items.title: A fan or compressor motor on its way out
items.text: A noisy or slow-spinning motor is a warning. Replacing one early is a smaller job than replacing it after it quits.

items.title: A thermostat that isn't talking to the unit
items.text: A blank screen, dead batteries or a bad connection can look like a failed air conditioner. It is worth ruling out first.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace Your Air Conditioner?
body: Here is a rule you can check yourself. If it's a capacitor, a motor or a coil that needs cleaning, repair is the answer, and it costs a fraction of a new system.
If the unit is old, the repairs keep coming or the compressor has failed, that is when to price a new one. A big repair bill on an old unit is often money better put toward a replacement.

We lay out both sides and tell you which one you're on, including when the answer is to repair. When it is time to replace, we install new air conditioning systems, and financing is available upon approval.

sections.heading: Four Things to Check Before You Call
body: If you can do it safely, a few quick checks can save a visit, or at least give us more to go on when you call.
list: The thermostat: is it set to cool, and are the batteries fresh?
The breaker for the outdoor unit: has it tripped?
The filter: if it's gray and packed with dust, change it and give the system an hour.
The outdoor unit: clear any grass, leaves or stacked items from around it.

why: Your AC repair page promises 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year, with someone answering the phone night and day. Your contact page says Monday to Saturday, 7 to 5, and closed Sunday. Someone whose AC quits on a Sunday can't tell which one is true, and that is the call you most need to win.

The headline at the top of your homepage is a long run of keywords ending in Lincoln, Nebraska, and 12 of your 16 pages carry the same one. Google can't tell which page is for what. Your reviews say it plainly: another company in town wanted a whole new system, and you found the fix. Today those words live on Google, not on your site.

So the demo tells one story on every page: look for the fix first, replace only when it's time. It opens with HVAC company in Lincoln, NE, and gives AC repair its own page, because that is the call people make on the hottest day.

lead.heading: Why we led with fixing it first
lead.text: The scariest moment for a Lincoln homeowner is hearing you need a whole new system and not knowing if it's true. Looking for the fix first answers that, and it rests on things Google can't find anywhere else: your customers' own accounts and the way you work on a call. That is also why it can help you rank, and please tell us if it isn't how you work.
